title: Staggered warmup waveform probe
content:
Summary:

Short: this is a working log for a set of microbenchmarks that exercise staggered (waveform) warmup/prefetch strategies for the KV cache to reduce NVMe/DRAM bandwidth spikes during multi-tenant cold-starts. Goal is to increase effective reuse while avoiding short-lived eviction storms that cause paging tail latency.

Why this experiment: 
- We observe that many production surges (small concurrent requests with long seqlen tails) cause a short high-bandwidth burst that overwhelms the NVMe channel and results in 10–100x p99 token latency spikes.
- Hypothesis: spreading KV page loads over a short waveform (staggered warmup) reduces instantaneous BW without materially hurting reuse for subsequent tokens, and reduces eviction thrash by avoiding synchronized warmup across worker threads.

Experiment design (high level):
1) Baseline: synchronous prefetch on request start (current prod behavior). Bench workload: mixed multi-tenant traces (10 tenants, 80/20 single/multi-turn), burst arrival model (poisson with microbursts).
2) Waveform-stagger: divide warmup into N micro-waves per request (N=4,8). On warmup trigger, issue prefetches in spaced batches using jitter schedule (linearly increasing spacing over first 20–80ms).
3) Heuristic-slim: aggressive LRU admission disabled for first 200ms after warmup to reduce immediate evictions of recently pinned pages.

Hardware and setup:
- Cluster: 4x nodes, each node has 8x A100 80GB (serving processes pinned), local NVMe 2TB, DDR5 host memory 1TB.
- Runtime: release/serve-1.14 (kv-prefetch branch), kernel: 6.1 tuned, io_uring enabled.
- Workload generator: replay traces from /data/traces/multi-tenant-2024-q4, scaled to 2k rps peak per node.
- Metrics: token latency (p50/p95/p99), KV hit rate (per-request reuse ratio), NVMe read MB/s (instantaneous sampling 10ms), DRAM read GB/s, eviction events/sec, CPU steal/backoff counts.

Key new metric: prefetch alignment variance (PAV)
- Definition: standard deviation of wallclock offsets between prefetch completion times and the first token consumption of that page. Low PAV means prefetchs are well aligned with actual use; high PAV implies wasted early loads or late arrivals. We use PAV@window(100ms) and PAV@window(1s).

Results (aggregated across 4 nodes):
- Baseline (sync prefetch): p50 token = 8.6ms, p95 = 46ms, p99 = 420ms; NVMe peak = 14500 MB/s, avg = 5200 MB/s; eviction events/sec = 820; KV reuse ratio = 0.42; PAV(100ms)=170ms (high).
- Waveform N=4 (linear spacing 0..40ms): p50 = 9.2ms (+7%), p95 = 38ms (-17%), p99 = 180ms (-57%); NVMe peak = 7800 MB/s (-46%), avg = 4100 MB/s; eviction events/sec = 330 (-60%); KV reuse ratio = 0.40 (-5%); PAV(100ms)=55ms (much lower).
- Waveform N=8 (spacing 0..80ms): p50 = 10.1ms (+17%), p95 = 36ms (-22%), p99 = 170ms (-60%); NVMe peak = 5400 MB/s (-63%), avg = 3800 MB/s; eviction events/sec = 250 (-70%); KV reuse ratio = 0.38 (-10%); PAV(100ms)=38ms.
- Heuristic-slim + Waveform N=8: p50 = 9.8ms, p95 = 34ms, p99 = 150ms; eviction events/sec = 140 (-83% vs baseline); KV reuse ratio = 0.43 (+2% vs baseline).

Interpretation: 
- Staggering warmup (waveform) trades a small p50 penalty (microseconds tens) for large reductions in p99 and NVMe peak bandwidth. That drop in peaks reduces eviction storms and paging amplification.
- There is an inflection: increasing N beyond ~8 returns diminishing NVMe benefit but adds p50 cost due to delayed page readiness. N=4..8 seems sweet spot for these traces.
- The heuristic-slim (relaxed admission immediately after warmup) recovers reuse and further reduces eviction counts — suggests eviction policy coupling is a major secondary effect.

Micro-observations / traces:
- On baseline traces, eviction bursts are tightly time-correlated with NVMe read spikes. Flamegraphs show CPU stalls in host prefetch worker threads at the same time as io_uring completions backlog.
- Waveform reduces IO completion backpressure and the scheduler shows fewer prefetch thread wakeups (lower CPU overhead by ~12%).
- PAV correlates strongly with p99; lowering PAV (more accurate alignment) tracks p99 improvements. In practice PAV can be used as a quick diagnostic without full tail-latency tracking.

Questions / unknowns: 
- How waveform interacts with multi-tenant fairness policies (we observed some tenants with aggressive patterns saw slightly reduced reuse). Need tenant-aware weighting.
- Stability under longer sustained peaks (12+ minutes) — NVMe warm cache behaviors changed after 6 minutes in one run (temperature throttling?), need longer runs.
- Sensitivity to SSD controller QoS: different NVMe models with different queue depths behaved differently; replicate on partner hardware.

Next steps / TODOs: 
- Re-run with tenant-weighted waveform: give higher-priority tenants earlier waves (sketch: priority factor alpha -> negative offset). (owner: Marcus) (JIRA-ENG-1432).
- Add PAV to production telemetry, expose PAV per-route in Console. (owner: Priya).
- Run 30m long soak on a mix including very long seqlen tails to observe thermal/SSD steady-state. (owner: Ethan).
- Prototype a lightweight admission flag triggered by waveform completion to delay eviction of newly-warmed pages for 200ms (this was the heuristic-slim above) — measure cross-tenant fairness.

Implementation notes (where code lives):
- Waveform scheduler: serve/runtime/kv/waveform_scheduler.{cc,py} (prototype in branch 'kv/waveform-wip').
- Waveform probe script: github.com/redwood-inference/serve-tools/kv/waveform_probe.py (in linked_artifacts). Use --replay-trace and --waveform-config to reproduce.
- Telemetry: added fields kv_prefetch_start, kv_prefetch_complete, kv_page_first_use_offset, eviction_reason to the profiling pipe. Sampling at 10ms buckets.

Quick checklist for reproducibility: 
- Checkout branch: git checkout kv/waveform-wip; build with debug telemetry on.
- Load traces: ./tools/trace_loader --trace /data/traces/multi-tenant-2024-q4 --scale 1.2
- Run probe: python serve-tools/kv/waveform_probe.py --nodes 4 --waveform-n 8 --spacing-ms 80 --metrics-out waveform-n8-run1.json

Notes to self / loose ideas: 
- Consider adaptive waveform: increase spacing when NVMe instantaneous BW > threshold, collapse spacing when BW drops (closed-loop). But carefully bound the adaptation rate to avoid oscillation.
- Test mixing waveform with prefix-KV pinning: pin top-k hot pages for 1s after warmup and let waveform handle the rest.
- Investigate kernel io_uring tuning: completion throttling seemed to interact with our prefetch pattern; maybe tune ring size or use batching in completions.

Appendix (raw interesting numbers from run 2024-11-20):
- Baseline p99 tail spike timeseries: 9 spikes in 20m window, avg spike duration 2.6s, mean p99 during spike = 1.2s.
- Waveform N=8 p99 spikes: 1 spike in 20m window, duration 1.1s, mean p99 during spike = 0.32s.
- Snapshot NVMe read histogram (samples/10ms): baseline 95th tile = 13700 MB/s, waveform 95th tile = 5200 MB/s.

If you want to discuss tradeoffs I can distill into a short doc for eng-review / infra launch checklist. For now this is a lab diary and the code is in the branch referenced above.
